rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1, 3.1 and 3.3 - the authors deployed their own IoT monitoring/decision-support system on eight drip-irrigated olive parcels in eastern Crete (2021-2022), sampled and analysed soils (Table 1), collected soil-moisture/EC/temperature and weather data, and compared the platform's weekly irrigation-dose recommendations with manually computed FAO-56 values during the 2022 irrigation season.
rows.notes: The study shows that the platform computes a weekly irrigation dose per tree (FAO-56 Penman-Monteith plus soil-moisture threshold check) and sends e-mail alerts, and that these recommended doses were identical to manually calculated FAO-56 values for all parcels in 2022 (Section 3.3). It does not measure applied irrigation volumes, water savings, water-use efficiency or yield, nor compare farmer water use with and without the platform; statements that the system 'can contribute to increased water-use efficiency' are assertions. The calculation of water requirements is only a precondition of the claimed efficient water use, so Q2 is 'no' and upstream is set. Limitations stated (Section 3.3: preliminary user testing, need for systematic user test, single crop) concern usability, not a water-conservation result; no dispersion statistics are given for any irrigation outcome.

notes: Full text appears complete though the OCR has duplicated/overlapping lines in several places (pages 4, 7-9, 12-14). The paper is a system design and implementation report; its only evaluative result is the agreement between platform-recommended doses/alerts and manual calculations, with no field measurement of water use or savings.
